steps.scene: You're emerging from a side road. There's a STOP sign and a solid white line across your lane, and the main road looks empty.

options.text: Slow right down and roll out if it's clear
Stop at the line every time, then look and emerge
Stop only if you can see traffic coming

question.explanation: A STOP sign is used where your view is restricted. You must stop at the line — the traffic you can't see is the point.

steps.title: The one octagon
steps.body: STOP is the only octagonal sign. Its shape alone identifies it, so it still works when snow or dirt hides the face.

question.prompt: Snow has covered the face of an eight-sided sign ahead. What is it?

options.text: A stop sign — no other sign is that shape
Impossible to tell until you can read the face
A give-way sign — they're the odd-shaped ones

question.explanation: Sign shapes carry meaning on their own. The octagon is reserved for STOP so it survives snow, dirt and a bad angle.

a.label: Solid stop line
a.body: With a STOP sign: you must stop completely at the line, every time.

b.label: Broken give-way line
b.body: At a give-way or roundabout entry: give way to traffic from the right, stop only if you must.

question.prompt: What does the broken line across a roundabout entry mean?

options.text: Stop at the line whether or not it's clear
Give way to traffic coming from your right
You have priority onto the roundabout

question.explanation: The line type tells you the rule: solid means stop, broken means give way. Stay behind it until it's safe to emerge.

steps.title: Hazard warning line
steps.body: When the centre-line marks become longer than the gaps, it's a hazard warning line. Something is coming up — don't start an overtake.

question.prompt: The centre line ahead changes to long marks with short gaps. This means…

options.text: An ordinary lane marking
A hazard ahead — look well ahead, don't overtake
A bus lane starts here

question.explanation: Long marks, short gaps = hazard warning line. It flags an unspecified hazard, so it's the wrong place to overtake or turn.

steps.title: Zigzags at a crossing
steps.body: White zigzags mark the approach to and exit from a pedestrian crossing. No parking at any time, and no overtaking the lead vehicle.

question.prompt: What do the white zigzag lines at a crossing mean?

options.text: No parking at any time
Parking allowed for a short drop-off
Sound your horn before the crossing

question.explanation: Parking on zigzags hides pedestrians from approaching drivers — that's why it's banned, along with overtaking there.

steps.scene: You reach a busy crossroads and the traffic lights are dead — no light showing in any direction.

options.text: Traffic on the main road keeps priority
Nobody — treat it as an unmarked crossroads
Traffic going straight ahead

question.explanation: With the lights out, no one has priority. Approach ready to stop and expect others to assume the right of way.

steps.wrongBelief: Signs and traffic lights always outrank a person directing traffic.

options.text: It's right — only the lights are legally binding
You must obey a police officer or warden directing traffic
Their signals apply only to buses and lorries

question.explanation: When an officer, traffic officer or warden directs traffic, their signals take over — obey them, whatever the lights show.

steps.repairNote: A police officer, traffic officer, traffic warden or school crossing patrol overrides the signs and lights — you must obey them.
